content: Ethinyl estradiol, also referred to as 17α-ethinylestradiol, is a synthetic derivative of 17β-estradiol (E2), which is the primary endogenous estrogen in humans. Ethinyl estradiol is an orally bioactive estrogen that is widely used in various formulations of combined oral contraceptive pills. It is one of the most commonly prescribed medications for contraception. When administered transdermally, ethinyl estradiol is associated with a higher risk of clot formation and venous thromboembolism compared to naturally occurring 17β-estradiol. This increased risk is hypothesized to be due to differences in hepatic metabolism following absorption. The same contraindications and precautions that apply to other estrogen medications also apply to ethinyl estradiol. A preparation of ethinyl estradiol alone, marketed under the name Estinyl, was previously used for the treatment of menopausal symptoms and female hypogonadism. However, ethinyl estradiol is excreted into the environment as a xenoestrogen through the urine and feces of individuals taking it as a medication. A significant concern with unopposed estrogen therapy (estrogen without progestogen) is the increased risk of endometrial cancer. Therefore, in the context of birth control, ethinyl estradiol is typically prescribed in combination with a progestin. Ethinyl estradiol was the first orally active semi-synthetic steroidal estrogen. It was synthesized in 1938 by Hans Herloff Inhoffen and Walter Hohlweg at Schering AG in Berlin. It was marketed as Estinyl starting on June 25, 1943. However, the FDA withdrew approval for Estinyl effective June 4, 2004, at the request of Schering, which had discontinued its marketing. Estradiol (E2) is readily absorbed when taken orally, but it is rapidly inactivated by the liver. The substitution of an ethinyl group at the C17 position of the estrane steroid structure makes ethinyl estradiol much more resistant to hepatic degradation. This modification was a key development in the creation of oral contraceptives. Ethinyl estradiol is absorbed in the small intestine, with serum levels peaking approximately two hours after ingestion. It undergoes extensive metabolism in the liver, primarily via the cytochrome P450 3A4 enzyme. Both ethinyl estradiol and its metabolites are excreted in the bile. Due to enterohepatic circulation, a secondary serum peak is observed several hours later. Medications such as antibiotics that interfere with enterohepatic circulation or liver enzymes can affect the pharmacokinetics of ethinyl estradiol. In circulation, ethinyl estradiol is almost entirely bound to plasma albumin. It is metabolized through hydroxylation of the aromatic ring and is excreted in both feces and urine, partly as glucuronide and sulfate conjugates. Ethinyl estradiol exerts its hormonal effects by activating estrogen receptors, making it a potent estrogen. Its most common use is in estrogen-progestin combination preparations for oral contraceptives. Over time, the dosage of ethinyl estradiol in these formulations has been reduced significantly, from as high as 100 μg in earlier products to as low as 10 μg in modern formulations such as Lo Loestrin Fe.
